tfn.s: Taking orders and meeting deadlines can make a hobby feel like a job.
tfn.why: The text says: "But taking orders, dealing with customers and meeting deadlines can turn a relaxing activity into another job."

tfn.s: Most people who sell their crafts give up within a year.
tfn.why: Not stated. The text does not say how long people keep selling their crafts.

tfn.s: Setting goals never helps anybody to improve.
tfn.why: The text says the opposite: "Setting goals helps some people improve, and selling something you have made can be exciting."

tfn.s: A 2026 Forbes article looked at making money from a hobby.
tfn.why: The text says: "In a 2026 Forbes article, a writer explored both the opportunities and the difficulties of making money from a hobby."

tfn.s: The text says the two friends who play guitar enjoy the hobby in the same way.
tfn.why: The text says: "Both can enjoy the same hobby in very different ways."

focus.note: A phrasal verb is a verb plus a small word, like set up. The small word changes the meaning, so learn the two words together.

Even when it rained, the runners carried ____ until they reached the end.

tfn.s: Everybody can afford to keep leisure completely separate from income.
tfn.why: The text says the opposite: "It would be unfair to suggest that everybody can afford to keep leisure completely separate from income."

tfn.s: The Forbes article proves that more people are turning hobbies into businesses.
tfn.why: The text says it is "practical business advice rather than research proving a trend".

tfn.s: Most hobby businesses make a loss in the first year.
tfn.why: The text says nothing about how much money hobby businesses earn or lose.

tfn.s: Seeing only exceptional achievements online can make ordinary enjoyment seem not good enough.
tfn.why: Exceptional achievements are "more visible than ordinary pleasure", and the second runner may feel enjoyment without improvement is "inadequate".

tfn.s: The text accepts that setting targets can be a healthy part of a hobby.
tfn.why: The text says: "There is nothing wrong with ambition" and "Sometimes competition is exciting and progress matters."

focus.note: The small word in a phrasal verb often changes the whole meaning. Read the full sentence before you choose.

items.s: Without meaning to, she ended ____ spending every weekend at craft fairs.

tfn.s: The writer suggests that a person's finances can affect how freely they choose to keep a hobby unpaid.
tfn.why: Someone with secure finances "might freely choose" to paint unpaid, while another person's "regular income is inadequate".

tfn.s: The Forbes article is presented as evidence that hobbies are becoming more commercial.
tfn.why: The text says: "It is business advice, not evidence of a social trend".

tfn.s: The text reveals how many people now earn money from a side hustle.
tfn.why: The text gives no figures about how many people have a side hustle.

tfn.s: The text implies that online comparison can affect both runners and people with creative projects.
tfn.why: A slow run is compared with recorded performances, and a private creative project can look disappointing beside an online portfolio.

tfn.s: The writer thinks a hobby that turns into paid work has necessarily lost its value.
tfn.why: The text says an activity may move "towards paid work" and that the meaningful distinction is whether changes are "chosen or imposed".

focus.note: Some phrasal verbs need an extra preposition after the particle, as in run out of or look down on. Learn the whole chunk, not only the two words.

Anyone who dislikes the pressure of rankings can simply opt ____ of the leaderboard.

speak.title: Role-play: should you sell your cakes?
speak.setup: Work in pairs. Read your card, then have the conversation. Swap roles and do it again.

a.text: You love your friend's cakes and think they should open an online shop. Give at least two reasons. Listen to their worries and answer them.

b.text: You bake for fun and your friend says you should sell your cakes. You are not sure. Explain what you enjoy now and what worries you.

phrases: I'd love to, but I'm worried it'd feel like work.
I bake because it's relaxing, not because I want money.
We could start small and see how it goes.
That's a fair point, I hadn't thought of that.
speak.after: Afterwards, tell the class: did the baker decide to sell, and what made the difference?
